Thus the Earth was added to the roster of planets,[[182]](#cite_note-galileo_project-183) and the Sun was removed. In March 1945, US bombers [destroy most of Kobe](/wiki/Bombing_of_Kobe "Bombing of Kobe") during the waning days of the [Pacific War](/wiki/Pacific_War "Pacific War"). Seita and his sister Setsuko, children of an [Imperial Japanese Navy](/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Navy "Imperial Japanese Navy") captain, survive, but their mother dies. She is cremated in a mass grave outside and Seita is seen carrying a small wooden box containing her ashes. Seita conceals their mother's death from Setsuko. The siblings move in with an aunt. He hides his mother's box of ashes in the garden. Seita retrieves a supply cache he buried before the bombing and gives everything to his aunt, save for a tin of [Sakuma drops](/wiki/Sakuma_drops "Sakuma drops"), which he gives to Setsuko. **[American Sign Language](/wiki/American_Sign_Language "American Sign Language")** (ASL) is the native language of a number of [deaf](/wiki/Deaf "Deaf") and hearing people in America (roughly 100,000 to 500,000). While some sources have stated that ASL is the third most frequently used language in the United States, after English and Spanish,[[134]](#cite_note-preston1995p243-138) recent scholarship has pointed out that most of these estimates are based on numbers conflating deafness with ASL use, and that the last actual study of this (in 1972) seems to indicate an upper bound of 500,000 ASL speakers at the time.[[135]](#cite_note-gallaudet2006-139)

* [Black American Sign Language](/wiki/Black_American_Sign_Language "Black American Sign Language") (BASL) developed in the southeastern United States, where separate residential schools were maintained for white and black deaf children. BASL shares much of the same vocabulary and grammatical structure as ASL and is generally considered one of its dialects.[[133]](#cite_note-EthnologueASL-137)[[134]](#cite_note-preston1995p243-138)[[136]](#cite_note-140)

**[Hawaiʻi Sign Language](/wiki/Hawai%CA%BBi_Sign_Language "Hawaiʻi Sign Language")** is moribund with only a handful of speakers on [Oʻahu](/wiki/O%CA%BBahu "Oʻahu"), [Lānaʻi](/wiki/L%C4%81na%CA%BBi "Lānaʻi"), [Kauaʻi](/wiki/Kaua%CA%BBi "Kauaʻi") and possibly [Niʻihau](/wiki/Ni%CA%BBihau "Niʻihau"). Sémillon, which is relatively easy to cultivate,[[3]](#cite_note-oxf-sem-3) consistently produces six to eight tons of grapes per acre from its vigorous vines.[[4]](#cite_note-pro-4) It is fairly resistant to disease, except for rot. The grape ripens early, when, in warmer climates, it acquires a pinkish hue.[[5]](#cite_note-cork-5) Since the grape has a thin skin, there is also a risk of sunburn in hotter climates; it is best suited to areas with sunny days and cool nights.

Sémillon wines are rather heavy, with low acidity and an almost oily texture. It has a high yield and wines based on it can age a long time. Along with [Sauvignon blanc](/wiki/Sauvignon_blanc "Sauvignon blanc") and [Muscadelle](/wiki/Muscadelle "Muscadelle"), Sémillon is one of only three approved white wine varieties in the [Bordeaux region](/wiki/Bordeaux_wine "Bordeaux wine").

The grape is also key to the production of sweet wines such as [Sauternes](/wiki/Sauternes_(wine) "Sauternes (wine)"). For the grapes to be used for sweet wine production, they need to have been affected by [Botrytis](/wiki/Botrytis_cinerea "Botrytis cinerea") (also known as "[noble rot](/wiki/Noble_rot "Noble rot")"). This fungus dries out the grapes, thus concentrating the sugar and flavours in the grape berry.

Titan orbits Saturn at 20 Saturn radii or 1,200,000 km above Saturn's apparent surface. From Titan's surface, Saturn, disregarding its [rings](/wiki/Rings_of_Saturn "Rings of Saturn"), subtends an arc of 5.09 degrees. When viewed from above its thick atmospheric haze it would appear 11.4 times larger in the sky, in diameter, than the Moon from Earth, which subtends 0.48° of arc.

Titan is primarily composed of ice and rocky material, with a rocky core surrounded by various layers of ice, including a crust of [ice Ih](/wiki/Ice_Ih "Ice Ih") and a subsurface layer of ammonia-rich liquid water. The [Catholic University of Leuven](/wiki/Catholic_University_of_Leuven_(1834%E2%80%931968) "Catholic University of Leuven (1834–1968)"), based in [Leuven](/wiki/Leuven "Leuven") ("*Louvain*" in French), 30 km east of [Brussels](/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), provided lectures in French from its founding in 1834, and in Dutch from 1930. In 1968, the [Dutch-language](/wiki/Dutch-language "Dutch-language") section became the independent [Katholieke Universiteit Leuven](/wiki/Katholieke_Universiteit_Leuven "Katholieke Universiteit Leuven"), which remained in Leuven, while the French-speaking university was expelled to a greenfield campus and town, [Louvain-la-Neuve](/wiki/Ottignies-Louvain-la-Neuve "Ottignies-Louvain-la-Neuve"), 30 km south-east of Brussels, in a part of the country where French is the official language. This separation also entailed dividing existing library holdings between the two new universities.

With the democratization of university education already stretching existing structures, plans to expand the French-speaking part of the university at a campus in [Brussels](/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") or [Wallonia](/wiki/Wallonia "Wallonia") were quietly discussed from the early 1960s, but it was not anticipated that the French-speaking section would become an entirely independent university and lose all of its buildings and infrastructure in [Leuven](/wiki/Leuven "Leuven"). The first stone of the new campus at Louvain-la-Neuve was laid in 1971, and the transfer of faculties to the new site was completed in 1979.
